Six reading passages (31 questions) and three cloze passages (16 blanks, one set error-based), all written for PrepMitra on themes not used in BATCH_000 to BATCH_005; the rest are standalone grammar, vocabulary and sentence-ordering items testing rules, words and idioms not tested in earlier batches. Each answer was set by the author and re-solved in a separate blind pass by fresh checkers without the key. Pending human review.

stimuli.title: Warning before the strike
stimuli.content:
Lightning kills more people in India each year than most other natural hazards, yet it rarely makes headlines. Unlike a cyclone or a flood, which can be tracked for days, a lightning strike is over in a fraction of a second, and its victims are usually scattered: a farmer in a field, a herder on a hillside, a group sheltering under a tree.

Most of these deaths happen in rural areas during the pre-monsoon and monsoon months, when thunderstorms build up quickly in the afternoon. People working outdoors are the most exposed. Many of them believe that a tall tree offers safety from the rain, but a lone tree is in fact one of the most dangerous places to stand, because lightning tends to strike the highest point in an open area.

In recent years, weather scientists have set up networks of sensors that detect the electrical activity of a storm as it forms. This allows them to issue warnings for a particular district from about thirty minutes to a few hours in advance. Several states now send these alerts as text messages, and free mobile apps show whether a storm is approaching the user's location.

A warning, however, is useful only if people know what to do with it. Officials therefore combine the alerts with simple advice. People caught outdoors should move into a solid building or a closed vehicle. If no shelter is near, they should keep away from trees, poles and water, and crouch low with their feet together rather than lie flat on the ground. They should also wait for about half an hour after the last thunder before going out again.

Experts say that awareness campaigns in schools and village meetings have already helped to reduce deaths in some districts. Their aim is modest but important: to turn a few minutes of warning into a few minutes of safe action.

stimuli.title: Money you can feel
stimuli.content:
For most people, telling one currency note from another takes only a glance. For the millions of Indians who are blind or have poor eyesight, it can be a daily struggle, and a mistake can be costly: a shopkeeper might hand back a ten-rupee note in place of a hundred, and the customer would never know.

Banknote designers try to help in several ways. Notes of different values are made in different sizes, so that a person can compare their length and width with the fingers. Many notes also carry marks printed in raised ink, such as small lines or shapes near the edge, which can be felt by touch. The large numerals and strong colours used on new notes are meant to help people whose sight is weak but not entirely lost.

These features do not always work as intended. When a new series of notes is introduced, older notes of the same value may stay in use for years, so people have to learn two sets of sizes. Raised printing tends to wear away as a note passes from hand to hand, and a note that has been folded, crumpled or soaked may be hard to read by touch at all. Some notes of neighbouring values are also so close in size that the difference is difficult to feel.

Technology now offers another aid. Mobile phone apps can identify a note when it is held in front of the camera and announce its value aloud, and some work even without an internet connection. Users say the apps are helpful, but they also point out that pulling out a phone for every transaction is slow, and not everyone owns a smartphone.

Organisations that work with the visually impaired argue that the best solution is a mix: notes designed with touch in mind from the very start, coins that are easy to tell apart, and apps for those who want them. Money, they say, should be usable by everyone who earns it.

stimuli.title: A number with a past
stimuli.content:
When a person stops using a mobile number, it does not disappear. After a period of inactivity, telecom operators may deactivate the connection and, some months later, issue the same number to a new customer. Numbers are a limited resource, and recycling them is a normal practice around the world. In an age of digital banking, however, it has created an unexpected risk.

Most bank accounts today are linked to a mobile number. The bank sends one-time passwords, transaction alerts and balance messages to that number, and many apps use it to identify the customer. If the old owner of a number forgets to update the bank, those messages may now reach a stranger. In the worst cases, a person who receives someone else's one-time passwords and has a few other details can reset passwords or approve payments.

The problem usually arises from neglect rather than crime. People change numbers when they move to a new city, switch operators or let a second SIM card lapse, and updating every bank, insurer and government service is tedious. Elderly customers and those who rarely use their accounts are especially likely to overlook it.

Banks and regulators have responded in several ways. Some banks now check whether a registered number has recently changed hands and ask the customer to confirm it before sending sensitive messages. Customers are urged to update their contact details whenever they give up a number, and to read alerts carefully, since an unfamiliar message may be the first sign that their details are out of date.

The episode is a reminder that security depends not only on strong technology but also on the ordinary links between a person and their accounts. A mobile number feels permanent to the person who uses it. To the network, it is merely on loan.

stimuli.title: Counting what hides
stimuli.content:
Counting tigers sounds simple until one tries it. The animals are shy, mostly active at night and spread across thick forest, so a direct head-count is impossible. For decades, Indian forest departments relied instead on pugmarks, the footprints that tigers leave on soft ground. Staff would trace the prints and try to tell individuals apart by their shape and size.

The method had obvious weaknesses. Prints change with the softness of the soil and the speed of the animal, and experts often disagreed over whether two prints came from one tiger or two. Critics argued that the counts tended to rise whenever officials were under pressure to show success.

Today the main tool is the camera trap: a weatherproof camera fixed to a tree, which takes a picture whenever an animal passes in front of it. Because the pattern of stripes on every tiger is unique, like a human fingerprint, a computer can match photographs and recognise individuals. Thousands of cameras are placed across a reserve for several weeks, and the results are analysed using a method known as capture-recapture.

The logic of capture-recapture is easiest to see with a simple example. Suppose cameras photograph forty different tigers in the first fortnight, and in the second fortnight they photograph forty again, of which twenty were already seen. Since half of the second sample had been 'captured' earlier, statisticians reason that the first sample probably represented about half the population, which is therefore around eighty. Real surveys use far more complex models, but the principle is the same.

Camera traps have drawbacks too. They are expensive, they can be stolen or damaged by elephants, and they work poorly for animals without distinctive markings. For such species, researchers increasingly turn to DNA extracted from droppings, which can identify individuals without the animal ever being seen.

What these methods share is a shift from guesswork to evidence that others can check. A count that can be repeated and verified, even if imperfect, is worth more than a confident figure that no one can test.

stimuli.title: The trouble with rent control
stimuli.content:
Few policies are as popular with voters, or as unpopular with economists, as rent control. When a city caps the rent that landlords may charge, tenants who already have homes are protected from sudden increases, and families who might otherwise be forced to move can stay near their schools and jobs. The appeal is easy to understand, especially in cities where rents have risen far faster than wages.

The difficulty lies in what happens next. If the permitted rent is well below what the market would bear, owning a flat to let becomes less rewarding. Some landlords sell their properties, others convert them into offices or holiday lets, and many simply leave flats empty rather than accept a low rent from a tenant they cannot easily remove. Builders, expecting controlled returns, put up fewer new rental homes. Over time, the supply of housing available for rent shrinks.

Those who already hold controlled tenancies benefit, often for decades. Newcomers to the city, who are frequently young and poor, find fewer homes on offer and may end up paying more in the uncontrolled part of the market or making informal payments to secure a flat. The policy thus divides tenants into insiders and outsiders, and the outsiders are not always better off than they would have been without it.

Maintenance suffers as well. A landlord who cannot raise the rent has little reason to repair a leaking roof, and tenants who fear losing a cheap flat are reluctant to complain. In some old city centres, buildings under long-standing rent control have decayed to the point of danger.

None of this means that tenants should be left at the mercy of the market. Many economists favour other remedies: allowing more homes to be built, offering housing allowances to poor families, or limiting how sharply rents may rise within an existing lease while letting them reset between tenants. Such measures are less eye-catching than a rent freeze, but they aim at the cause of high rents, a shortage of homes, rather than at its symptom.

stimuli.title: The month you were born
stimuli.content:
In many sports academies, a curious pattern appears when the players' birth dates are listed. Far more of them are born in the months just after the cut-off date used to group children by age than in the months just before it. The pattern has been found in football, cricket and ice hockey across several countries, and psychologists call it the relative age effect.

The explanation lies in the way children are sorted. If teams are formed by calendar year, a child born in January and one born in December of the same year play in the same age group, although the first is almost a year older. At the age of eight or nine, eleven months can make a large difference to height, strength and coordination. The older child is more likely to stand out in a trial, be picked for a better team and receive more coaching, which widens the gap still further. What began as an accident of the calendar is gradually mistaken for talent.

The effect does not stop at sport. Studies in several countries have found that, on average, the youngest children in a school class score slightly lower in early tests and are more often judged to have learning or behavioural difficulties. Much of this gap narrows as children grow older, but decisions taken early, such as placement in a slower stream, can have lasting consequences.

Curiously, the advantage is sometimes reversed at the highest level. A few studies suggest that among the relatively young players who do reach professional sport, a larger share go on to long careers, perhaps because they had to develop skill and resilience to compete with bigger rivals.

Remedies are simple in principle. Selectors can be shown each child's age in months and asked to judge performance against it; some academies have experimented with rotating the cut-off date each year, or with grouping children by physical development rather than birth date. None of these removes the effect entirely, but each reduces the chance that a selector confuses being older with being better.

stimuli.title: The many lives of bamboo
stimuli.content:
Bamboo is often called a tree, but it is in fact a giant grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on earth. Some species can grow (1) ______ a metre in a single day, and a new clump can be harvested within a few years, far sooner than most timber trees.

For centuries, rural communities in India's north-east have used bamboo for almost everything: houses, bridges, baskets, water pipes and even food, since its young shoots are cooked and eaten as a (2) ______. Because the plant regrows from its roots after cutting, a well-managed grove can supply material year after year without being (3) ______.

Bamboo's strength surprises many people. Weight for weight, some species are remarkably strong when pulled, which is why builders in parts of Asia still use bamboo poles for scaffolding on tall buildings. It is also light and (4) ______, so it bends in strong winds rather than snapping.

The plant does have limits. Untreated bamboo is easily attacked by insects and fungi, and it can rot within a few years if it is left in damp conditions. Simple treatments with salt solutions can extend its life many times over, but they are not yet widely (5) ______ by village craftsmen, many of whom have never been shown how to use them. Supporters argue that with better treatment and design, bamboo could replace some of the cement and steel used in rural housing, cutting both costs and the pollution that comes from making those materials.

stimuli.title: The real cost of free returns
stimuli.content:
Online shoppers have come to expect that anything they buy can be sent back free of charge. For retailers, generous return policies are a powerful way to (1) ______ customers who would otherwise hesitate to buy clothes or shoes they cannot try on. A buyer who knows she can return a dress is far more likely to order it, and perhaps to order two sizes at once.

The convenience, however, comes at a price that the shopper rarely sees. Every returned parcel must be collected, transported back to a warehouse, inspected and repackaged before it can be sold again. For low-priced goods, these steps can cost more than the item itself, so many returns are never put back on sale at all; they are sold off cheaply in bulk or simply (2) ______.

Returns also add to (3) ______. A parcel that travels to the customer and back again doubles the delivery journey, and the packaging used for it is often thrown away. Some estimates suggest that a significant share of everything bought online is returned, and the share is highest for (4) ______, where fit is hard to judge on a screen.

Retailers have begun to look for ways to reduce returns without losing customers. Better size charts, photographs taken from several angles and reviews that mention whether an item runs small or large all help buyers choose correctly the first time. A few companies have started to charge a small fee for returns, or to offer a discount to shoppers who (5) ______ to keep an item they are unsure about.

The broader lesson is that 'free' is seldom truly free. When a service costs the customer nothing, its cost is usually (6) ______ somewhere else, whether in higher prices, lower wages along the delivery chain, or a heavier burden on the environment.

stimuli.title: When rates rise, bonds fall
stimuli.content:
A government bond is a promise to pay its holder a fixed amount of interest every year and to return the original sum when the bond matures. Because the interest is fixed when the bond is issued, the bond's market price must **(1) adjust** whenever interest rates in the economy change.

Suppose a bond pays seven per cent a year, and soon afterwards new bonds are issued paying eight per cent. No investor will now pay full price for the old bond when a new one offers more, so the old bond's price must **(2) rise** until its fixed payments give a buyer roughly the same return as the new bonds. The opposite happens when rates fall: older bonds, paying more than new ones, become more **(3) attractive**, and their prices go up.

This is why bond prices and interest rates are said to be **(4) directly** related. The effect is strongest for bonds that have many years left to run, because their fixed payments stretch far into the future, so a change in rates affects a larger stream of income.

The relationship matters well beyond the bond market. Banks hold large amounts of government bonds, and a sharp rise in interest rates can reduce the value of these holdings and **(5) strengthen** their balance sheets. Investors and regulators therefore watch the expected path of interest rates closely, since even a small change can shift the value of portfolios worth billions. For an ordinary saver, the lesson is simpler: a bond held until it matures returns its full original sum, but one sold earlier may fetch less than was paid for it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why does lightning rarely make headlines?

options.text: It kills far fewer people than cyclones and floods do.
Each strike is over in an instant and its victims are scattered.
Most strikes happen at night when nobody is reporting.
Weather offices do not record deaths caused by lightning.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1 contrasts lightning with cyclones and floods, which 'can be tracked for days': a strike 'is over in a fraction of a second, and its victims are usually scattered'.
steps: The next sentence gives the reason
Over in a fraction of a second + scattered victims
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Kills far fewer people' contradicts the first sentence, which says lightning kills more than most other hazards. The passage says storms build up in the afternoon, not at night. Nothing is said about weather offices failing to record deaths.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Each strike is over in an instant and its victims are scattered.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, is a lone tree a dangerous place to stand during a thunderstorm?

options.text: Its branches may break and fall in the strong wind.
Rainwater collects around its roots and conducts current.
Lightning tends to strike the highest point in open ground.
Animals and insects gather under it to shelter from rain.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: a lone tree is one of the most dangerous places to stand 'because lightning tends to strike the highest point in an open area'.
steps: Highest point in an open area
solution.why_others_wrong: Falling branches, water around the roots and sheltering animals are never mentioned; they are guesses from general knowledge, not reasons given in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Lightning tends to strike the highest point in open ground.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT part of the advice given to people caught outdoors in a thunderstorm?

options.text: Lie flat on the ground until the storm passes.
Move into a solid building or a closed vehicle.
Keep away from trees, poles and water.
Wait about half an hour after the last thunder.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4 advises shelter in a solid building or closed vehicle, keeping away from trees, poles and water, crouching low with feet together 'rather than lie flat on the ground', and waiting half an hour after the last thunder. Lying flat is the one thing it tells people not to do.
steps: Away from trees, poles and water: stated
Half an hour after the last thunder: stated
solution.why_others_wrong: Shelter in a building or vehicle, keeping away from trees and water, and waiting half an hour are all stated in paragraph 4, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Lie flat on the ground until the storm passes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'exposed' as used in the passage ('People working outdoors are the most exposed')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: exposed (to a danger) = left without protection from it
solution.explanation: People in the open fields have nothing between them and the storm. 'Exposed' here means unprotected from the danger of lightning.
steps: They lack shelter from the danger
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Revealed' and 'displayed' are the senses of 'exposed' used for secrets or objects put on show. 'Experienced' has nothing to do with lacking protection.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: How, according to the passage, do notes of different sizes help a person who cannot see them?

options.text: Shopkeepers are required to count them out aloud.
Larger notes make a louder sound when they are shaken.
Smaller notes are printed in brighter, stronger colours.
The person can compare their length and width by touch.

solution.concept: Locating a stated purpose
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: notes of different values are made in different sizes 'so that a person can compare their length and width with the fingers'.
steps: Compare length and width by touch
solution.why_others_wrong: Sound and a duty on shopkeepers are never mentioned. Strong colours are mentioned, but for people with weak sight, and they are not linked to the size of the note.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The person can compare their length and width by touch.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT given in the passage as a reason why the touch features of notes do not always work?

options.text: Old and new notes of one value may circulate together.
Raised printing wears away as notes change hands.
Some neighbouring values are very close in size.
Raised marks are printed only on high-value notes.

solution.concept: Factual (NOT) question: eliminate every option the passage states
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 gives three problems: old and new series in use together, raised printing that wears away (or notes that are crumpled or soaked), and neighbouring values that are close in size. It never says raised marks appear only on high-value notes.
steps: Marks only on high-value notes: not in the passage
solution.why_others_wrong: The two series in circulation, worn raised printing and close sizes are all stated in paragraph 3, so none of them can be the answer.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Raised marks are printed only on high-value notes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What drawback of note-reading mobile apps do users point out?

options.text: They work only when there is an internet connection.
They often announce the wrong value for older notes.
Using a phone for every payment is slow, and not all own one.
They are sold at a price that most users cannot afford.

solution.concept: Locating a stated drawback
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: users 'point out that pulling out a phone for every transaction is slow, and not everyone owns a smartphone'.
steps: Two drawbacks: slow, and not everyone owns a smartphone
Match the option that states both
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says some apps work 'even without an internet connection', which rules out the first option. Wrong values and a high price are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Using a phone for every payment is slow, and not all own one.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

solution.concept: Title: the idea that runs through every paragraph
solution.explanation: Every paragraph deals with how people who cannot see well identify money: the problem, design features, their limits, apps and a mixed solution. The last line says money 'should be usable by everyone who earns it'.
steps: Para 1: the problem for blind people
solution.why_others_wrong: Fake notes and the decline of cash are not discussed. Coins are mentioned only once, in passing, and the passage has no history.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Making Money Usable for All

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, what may telecom operators do with a number that has been inactive for some time?

options.text: Sell it back to the bank to which it was linked
Deactivate it and later issue it to a new customer
Keep it blocked permanently for security reasons
Transfer it automatically to the owner's new phone

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'telecom operators may deactivate the connection and, some months later, issue the same number to a new customer'.
steps: Find 'After a period of inactivity' in paragraph 1
Deactivate, then reissue to someone new
solution.why_others_wrong: Selling numbers to banks and automatic transfer are never mentioned. Permanent blocking contradicts the statement that recycling numbers is normal practice.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Deactivate it and later issue it to a new customer

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which customers, according to the passage, are especially likely to forget to update their mobile number with the bank?

options.text: Young people who change phones every year
Customers who bank only at a branch counter
Elderly people and those who rarely use their accounts
Business owners who hold accounts in many banks

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'Elderly customers and those who rarely use their accounts are especially likely to overlook it.'
steps: Two groups: elderly customers, rare users
solution.why_others_wrong: Young people, branch-only customers and business owners are not singled out anywhere in the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Elderly people and those who rarely use their accounts

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'tedious' as used in the passage ('updating every bank, insurer and government service is tedious')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: tedious = long, dull and tiring
solution.explanation: Contacting every bank, insurer and government office one by one is a dull, drawn-out chore. 'Tedious' means tiresome.
steps: Context: updating many organisations one by one
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing in the sentence suggests that updating details is dangerous, expensive or against the law; the point is that it is a boring chore people put off.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author mean by saying that the problem 'usually arises from neglect rather than crime'?

options.text: Most cases begin with people forgetting to update details, not with a fraud plan.
Banks neglect their duty to customers far more often than criminals do.
Fraud with recycled numbers is rare because the police act quickly on it.
Customers who lose money this way are usually to blame and get no refund.

solution.concept: Inference: what a contrast ('neglect rather than crime') says about causes
solution.explanation: The sentences that follow explain the 'neglect': people change numbers and do not update every bank because it is tedious. So the usual starting point is forgetfulness by the old owner, not a deliberate scheme by criminals.
steps: The next sentences describe people failing to update details
Most cases start with forgetfulness, not a fraud plan
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage blames customers' forgetfulness, not banks, for the neglect. Police action is never mentioned. Blame and refunds are not discussed; the point is about how the problem starts.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Most cases begin with people forgetting to update details, not with a fraud plan.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author suggest by the closing line, 'To the network, it is merely on loan'?

options.text: Customers must pay a monthly fee to keep using their numbers.
A number belongs to the network and may pass to someone else.
Banks lend money only to customers with a registered number.
Telecom operators may withdraw a number if a loan is unpaid.

solution.concept: Inference: the meaning of a closing metaphor
solution.explanation: Something on loan is used for a while and then returned. The author contrasts how permanent a number feels to its user with the network's view: the number is only borrowed and can be reissued to a new customer, as paragraph 1 describes.
steps: 'feels permanent to the person' vs 'on loan' to the network
On loan = borrowed for a time, then reused
Links back to recycling in paragraph 1
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options take 'loan' literally as money or fees, which the passage never connects with mobile numbers.
solution.final_answer: Option B: A number belongs to the network and may pass to someone else.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why, according to the passage, is a direct head-count of tigers impossible?

options.text: Tigers are shy, mostly active at night and spread over thick forest.
Forest departments are not allowed to enter the core of a reserve.
Tigers move between reserves so often that they are counted twice.
Most reserves are too small to hold enough tigers to be counted.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 1: 'The animals are shy, mostly active at night and spread across thick forest, so a direct head-count is impossible.'
steps: Shy, nocturnal, spread over thick forest
solution.why_others_wrong: Restricted entry, movement between reserves and small reserves are never given as reasons; they are plausible guesses from outside the passage.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Tigers are shy, mostly active at night and spread over thick forest.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is given in the passage as a weakness of the pugmark method?

options.text: Tigers avoid walking on the soft ground where prints form.
Prints vary with soil and speed, so experts disagreed on them.
Tracing prints needed costly equipment that often broke down.
Prints were washed away before staff could reach the forest.

solution.concept: Locating a stated weakness
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Prints change with the softness of the soil and the speed of the animal, and experts often disagreed over whether two prints came from one tiger or two.'
steps: Prints change with soil and speed
solution.why_others_wrong: Paragraph 1 says tigers do leave prints on soft ground, so avoiding it is wrong. Costly equipment is a drawback of camera traps, not pugmarks. Washed-away prints are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Prints vary with soil and speed, so experts disagreed on them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the critics' argument in paragraph 2 suggest about the old tiger counts?

options.text: They were always lower than the true number of tigers.
They were produced by computers that matched footprints.
They may have reflected officials' wishes more than evidence.
They were checked every year by independent experts.

solution.concept: Inference: what an observed pattern implies
solution.explanation: If counts rose 'whenever officials were under pressure to show success', the numbers moved with the officials' needs, not only with the tigers. The critics were suggesting that the counts could be shaped by what officials wanted to report.
steps: Pattern: counts rose when officials needed success
The figure followed the pressure, not the forest
Counts may have reflected wishes rather than evidence
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Always lower' runs against the critics' point that counts tended to rise. Computers matching footprints mixes up the two methods. Independent yearly checks contradict the final paragraph, which praises the new methods because they can be checked.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They may have reflected officials' wishes more than evidence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Using the reasoning of the example in paragraph 4, what would be the estimated population if the cameras photographed forty tigers in each fortnight but only ten of the second forty had already been seen?

solution.concept: Inference: applying the capture-recapture logic to new figures
solution.explanation: Ten of forty is one quarter, so the first sample of forty is taken to be about one quarter of the population: 40 × 4 = 160. (Estimate = first sample × second sample ÷ recaptured = 40 × 40 ÷ 10.)
steps: Share of the second sample already seen: 10 of 40 = one quarter
So the first sample (40) is about one quarter of the population
solution.shortcut: Estimate = (first count × second count) ÷ number seen in both = 40 × 40 ÷ 10 = 160
solution.why_others_wrong: About eighty is the passage's own answer for twenty recaptures, not ten. About forty would mean every tiger was seen in the first fortnight. About one hundred and twenty does not follow from any of the figures; fewer recaptures mean a larger population, here four times the first sample.
solution.final_answer: Option D: about one hundred and sixty

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is closest in meaning to the word 'distinctive' as used in the passage ('they work poorly for animals without distinctive markings')?

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: distinctive = marking out one individual from others
solution.explanation: Camera traps work for tigers because each stripe pattern is unique, so individuals can be recognised. Animals without such markings cannot be told apart in photographs. 'Distinctive' therefore means easily told apart.
steps: Purpose of markings here: to recognise individuals
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Brightly coloured' confuses being noticeable with being individually recognisable. 'Permanently fixed' and 'widely admired' have nothing to do with telling one animal from another.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.text: Camera traps have made tiger counts perfectly accurate.
Pugmarks remain the cheapest and best way to count tigers.
Counts that others can check are worth more than confident guesses.
DNA from droppings will soon replace every other counting method.

solution.concept: Main idea: the author's conclusion in the last paragraph
solution.explanation: The passage moves from pugmarks to camera traps and DNA, and ends: 'A count that can be repeated and verified, even if imperfect, is worth more than a confident figure that no one can test.'
steps: Para 6: verifiable evidence beats confident guesses
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Perfectly accurate' contradicts 'even if imperfect' and the drawbacks in paragraph 5. The passage criticises pugmarks. DNA is offered for animals without markings, not as a replacement for every method.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Counts that others can check are worth more than confident guesses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the passage, why do builders put up fewer new rental homes under rent control?

options.text: They expect the returns on such homes to be held down.
They are legally barred from building rental housing.
They cannot find tenants willing to live in new flats.
They prefer to build schools and offices for the city.

solution.concept: Locating a stated reason
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'Builders, expecting controlled returns, put up fewer new rental homes.'
steps: Returns held down by the cap
solution.why_others_wrong: No legal bar is mentioned. A shortage of tenants contradicts the passage, which describes newcomers struggling to find homes. Converting flats to offices is something some landlords do, not the builders' reason.
solution.final_answer: Option A: They expect the returns on such homes to be held down.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What, according to the passage, do many landlords do rather than accept a low rent from a tenant they cannot easily remove?

options.text: They raise the rent quietly without telling the city.
They leave their flats standing empty.
They move into the flats themselves.
They hand the flats over to the city council.

solution.concept: Locating a stated fact
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'many simply leave flats empty rather than accept a low rent from a tenant they cannot easily remove'.
steps: Find 'rather than accept a low rent' in paragraph 2
solution.why_others_wrong: Raising rents secretly, moving in and handing flats to the council are not mentioned. The other actions the passage names are selling and converting to offices or holiday lets.
solution.final_answer: Option B: They leave their flats standing empty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the author imply by describing rent control as dividing tenants into 'insiders and outsiders'?

options.text: Tenants in the city centre pay more than those in the suburbs.
Insiders who complain about repairs are evicted and become outsiders.
Landlords favour tenants from inside the city over migrants from outside.
Existing tenants gain, while newcomers may face fewer homes and higher costs.

solution.concept: Inference: who gains and who loses from a policy
solution.explanation: Paragraph 3 says those who hold controlled tenancies benefit 'often for decades', while newcomers find fewer homes and may pay more or make informal payments. The 'insiders' are existing tenants; the 'outsiders' are newcomers who bear the cost.
steps: The policy's gains and losses fall on different groups
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage does not compare centre and suburbs, does not describe landlords choosing locals over migrants, and never says complaining tenants are evicted; it says tenants are reluctant to complain.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Existing tenants gain, while newcomers may face fewer homes and higher costs.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the phrase 'left at the mercy of the market' mean as used in the passage?

options.text: given generous help by local traders
allowed to bargain freely for better homes
left unprotected from whatever rents the market sets
forced to sell their homes at low prices

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: at the mercy of = without any protection against
solution.explanation: Having listed the harms of rent control, the author says this does not mean tenants should be left with no protection at all against market rents, and goes on to suggest other remedies. 'At the mercy of' means in the power of, unprotected from.
steps: 'None of this means ...' = the author still wants tenants protected
At the mercy of = powerless against
'left unprotected from whatever rents the market sets'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Generous help' takes 'mercy' in its everyday sense of kindness. 'Bargain freely' turns the phrase into a benefit. 'Forced to sell their homes' confuses tenants with owners.
solution.final_answer: Option C: left unprotected from whatever rents the market sets

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the author's attitude towards rent control?

options.text: enthusiastic, urging every city to adopt it at once
indifferent, treating housing as a purely private matter
critical of its effects, but sympathetic to tenants' needs
hostile to tenants, whom it blames for high rents

solution.concept: Tone: weigh criticism against the author's stated concern
solution.explanation: The author lists the policy's harms (fewer homes, insiders and outsiders, poor maintenance) but begins by explaining its appeal and ends by insisting that tenants should not be left at the mercy of the market, proposing other remedies.
steps: Para 1: its appeal is 'easy to understand'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Enthusiastic' contradicts the long list of harms. 'Indifferent' is wrong because the author proposes remedies. 'Hostile to tenants' is wrong because the author blames a shortage of homes, not tenants, for high rents.
solution.final_answer: Option C: critical of its effects, but sympathetic to tenants' needs

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: According to the author, how do the remedies favoured by many economists differ from a rent freeze?

options.text: They help landlords rather than tenants.
They take effect faster than a freeze.
They tackle the shortage of homes behind high rents.
They cost the government nothing at all.

solution.concept: Inference: the contrast drawn in the final sentence
solution.explanation: The last sentence says such measures 'aim at the cause of high rents, a shortage of homes, rather than at its symptom'. A rent freeze treats the symptom (high rents); the remedies address the cause.
steps: The remedies aim at that cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Housing allowances for poor families and limits within a lease help tenants. Speed is not discussed, and housing allowances clearly cost the government money.
solution.final_answer: Option C: They tackle the shortage of homes behind high rents.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the process explained in paragraph 2?

options.text: A small early advantage grows because it attracts more opportunities.
Talent shown at eight or nine years predicts adult success exactly.
Children born in December train harder to make up for their age.
Coaches deliberately choose older children to win junior matches.

solution.concept: Inference: identifying a self-reinforcing process
solution.explanation: The older child stands out, is picked for a better team and gets more coaching, 'which widens the gap still further'. A small head start produces chances that make it larger: a self-reinforcing advantage.
steps: Start: up to eleven months' physical head start
Result: selection, better team, more coaching
'widens the gap still further' = the advantage feeds itself
solution.why_others_wrong: The passage says the early edge is 'mistaken for talent', not that it predicts adult success. Harder training by younger children appears only as a guess about professionals in paragraph 4. Nothing says coaches act deliberately; the point is that they confuse age with ability.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A small early advantage grows because it attracts more opportunities.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Why does the author say that 'an accident of the calendar is gradually mistaken for talent'?

options.text: Parents falsify birth dates so that their children seem talented.
Children born in some months are genetically more gifted at sport.
Academies change their calendars so that talented players fit in.
Selectors read the physical edge of being older as natural ability.

solution.concept: Inference: interpreting a key sentence from its context
solution.explanation: Being born just after the cut-off is chance (an 'accident of the calendar'). The extra size and strength it gives is judged in trials as talent, and further coaching then makes the gap look like real ability.
steps: 'accident of the calendar' = the chance of birth month
Its effect: greater height, strength, coordination
Selectors take that edge for talent
solution.why_others_wrong: Genetic gifts contradict the passage's explanation, which is relative age, not birth month as such. Academies changing calendars and parents falsifying dates are never mentioned.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Selectors read the physical edge of being older as natural ability.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What do a few studies suggest about relatively young players who reach professional sport?

options.text: They usually retire early because of injuries.
They are paid less than players born earlier.
A larger share of them go on to long careers.
Most of them were born just after the cut-off.

solution.concept: Locating a stated finding
solution.explanation: Paragraph 4: 'among the relatively young players who do reach professional sport, a larger share go on to long careers'.
steps: Find 'reversed at the highest level' in paragraph 4
Finding: a larger share have long careers
solution.why_others_wrong: Early retirement and lower pay are not mentioned. 'Born just after the cut-off' describes the relatively old players, the opposite group.
solution.final_answer: Option C: A larger share of them go on to long careers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: A cricket academy groups boys by calendar year of birth. Which change would the author most likely support?

options.text: Selecting only boys born between January and March
Holding trials only for boys taller than a fixed height
Judging each boy's performance against his age in months
Excluding boys born in December from the selection trials

solution.concept: Inference: applying the author's remedies to a new case
solution.explanation: The last paragraph proposes showing selectors 'each child's age in months' and asking them to judge performance against it, so that being older is not confused with being better.
steps: Problem: older boys in the group look better
Author's remedy: judge performance against age in months
solution.why_others_wrong: Selecting only early-born boys, a height bar and excluding December boys would all strengthen the bias against younger or smaller children, which the author wants to reduce.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Judging each boy's performance against his age in months

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: What does the word 'stream' mean as used in the passage ('decisions taken early, such as placement in a slower stream, can have lasting consequences')?

options.text: a small river running through a valley
a steady line of thought or argument
a continuous flow of data online
a group of pupils taught by ability

solution.concept: Vocabulary in context: stream (in schools) = a class or group of pupils of similar ability
solution.explanation: The sentence is about decisions taken in school for children judged to be weaker. Being placed in a 'slower stream' means being put in a group of pupils taught at a slower pace according to ability.
steps: Context: school decisions about young pupils
'a group of pupils taught by ability'
solution.why_others_wrong: A river, a flow of data and a line of thought are other senses of 'stream' that make no sense with 'placement in a slower ...' in a school.
solution.final_answer: Option D: a group of pupils taught by ability

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?

options.text: How to Build a Cricket Academy

solution.concept: Title: the central idea of the whole passage
solution.explanation: The passage shows how being older within an age group is mistaken for being better, in sport and in school, and ends with remedies that reduce 'the chance that a selector confuses being older with being better'.
steps: Paras 1–3: older children are taken to be more able
Para 4: the effect can even reverse
Para 5: stop confusing older with better
solution.why_others_wrong: 'How to Build a Cricket Academy' is too narrow. Sleep is never discussed. 'Why Talent Is Inherited' contradicts the passage, which explains the pattern by age, not inheritance.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Older Is Not Always Better

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the word must agree with 'one of the fastest-growing plants'
solution.explanation: The sentence illustrates how fast bamboo grows, so it must describe a large amount: some species grow nearly a metre in a day.
steps: Claim just made: one of the fastest-growing plants
The example must show great speed
'grow nearly a metre in a single day'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hardly a metre' would play down the growth and clash with 'fastest-growing'. 'Seldom' and 'never' do not fit before a quantity and would contradict the claim.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'cooked and eaten as a ...' needs a kind of food
solution.explanation: The list ends with 'even food', and the shoots are 'cooked and eaten'. Something cooked and eaten as a special food is a delicacy.
solution.why_others_wrong: Fuel and decoration are not eaten. 'Medicine' does not answer 'even food', the item the sentence is explaining.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'regrows from its roots' means the supply is not used up
solution.explanation: Because bamboo regrows after cutting, a grove can be cut year after year without being used up: without being exhausted.
steps: Cause: the plant regrows from its roots
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Without being harvested' contradicts 'supply material year after year', which requires cutting. 'Planted' and 'watered' do not express the idea of a supply that lasts.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'so it bends ... rather than snapping' explains the blank
solution.explanation: Something that bends instead of breaking is flexible.
steps: Result clause: bends rather than snapping
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Rigid' and 'brittle' describe materials that do not bend and are likely to snap. 'Heavy' contradicts 'light' earlier in the same sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the reason given after the blank decides the word
solution.explanation: The treatments work, but craftsmen 'have never been shown how to use them'. So the treatments are not yet widely taken up: not yet widely adopted.
steps: Reason: craftsmen have never been shown how to use them
Not yet taken up = 'not yet widely adopted'
solution.why_others_wrong: Craftsmen who have never been shown a method cannot have 'opposed', 'abandoned' or 'criticised' it widely; those words also do not follow from a lack of training.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (1). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the purpose of a generous return policy
solution.explanation: Customers who would otherwise hesitate are won over by the promise of free returns. The policy is a way to attract them.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Deter' and 'penalise' are the opposite of a 'powerful way' to win hesitant buyers. 'Refund customers' does not explain why they would now buy.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (2). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: what happens to returns that are 'never put back on sale'
solution.explanation: Goods that are never sold again are either sold off cheaply in bulk or simply thrown away: discarded.
steps: Clue: 'never put back on sale at all'
First outcome: sold off cheaply in bulk
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Displayed' and 'delivered' contradict 'never put back on sale'. 'Upgraded' would add cost to goods whose return already costs more than they are worth.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (3). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: the sentences after the blank explain it
solution.explanation: The paragraph describes doubled delivery journeys and packaging that is thrown away, both of which harm the environment. Returns add to pollution.
steps: Next sentence: doubled journeys, wasted packaging
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Loyalty', 'savings' and 'accuracy' are benefits, which do not match the costs described next and the passage's point that the convenience 'comes at a price'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (4). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: 'where fit is hard to judge on a screen'
solution.explanation: Fit matters for things that are worn. Paragraph 1 also mentions clothes and shoes that buyers 'cannot try on'. The share of returns is highest for clothing.
steps: Clue: 'where fit is hard to judge'
Para 1: clothes and shoes buyers cannot try on
solution.why_others_wrong: Groceries, medicines and books do not have a 'fit' to judge, so the clue after the blank does not apply to them.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (5). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: a discount rewards the behaviour the retailer wants
solution.explanation: Retailers want fewer returns, so they reward shoppers who choose to keep an item: shoppers who agree to keep it.
steps: A discount rewards keeping the item
'shoppers who agree to keep an item'
solution.why_others_wrong: Retailers would not reward shoppers who 'refuse' or 'hesitate' to keep an item, since that leads to returns. 'Forget to keep' is meaningless here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, a word is missing at the blank numbered (6). Choose the word that best fits the blank.

solution.concept: Cloze: collocation 'a cost is borne (by someone)'
solution.explanation: If a service is free to the customer, someone else still pays: the cost is borne (carried) elsewhere, as the list of higher prices, lower wages and environmental burden shows.
steps: The cost still falls on someone else
'its cost is usually borne somewhere else'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Avoided', 'cancelled' and 'reduced' would mean the cost disappears or shrinks, contradicting 'free is seldom truly free' and the list of places where it shows up.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (1) may be wrongly used: 'Because the interest is fixed when the bond is issued, the bond's market price must adjust whenever interest rates in the economy change'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the 'Because' clause explains why the price must change
solution.explanation: The interest payment cannot change, so when rates in the economy move, the only thing that can change is the bond's price. The price must adjust. 'Adjust' is correct.
steps: So the price has to change when rates change
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Remain' says the price stays the same, the opposite of what the passage goes on to describe. 'Vanish' and 'double' are extreme changes that the passage never describes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (2) may be wrongly used: 'No investor will now pay full price for the old bond when a new one offers more, so the old bond's price must rise'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: follow the logic of 'No investor will now pay full price'
solution.explanation: If nobody will pay full price for the old bond, its price has to come down until its fixed seven per cent gives a buyer about the same return as a new eight per cent bond. The price must fall, not rise.
steps: Nobody will pay full price for the old bond
So its price must go down
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Double' and 'rise' move the price the wrong way. 'Stabilise' ignores the need for the price to drop. 'Rise' is wrong, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (3) may be wrongly used: 'older bonds, paying more than new ones, become more attractive, and their prices go up'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: the participle phrase gives the reason
solution.explanation: When rates fall, older bonds pay more than new ones, so investors want them more. Being more attractive, their prices go up. 'Attractive' is correct.
steps: Older bonds now pay more than new ones
solution.why_others_wrong: Nothing in the sentence makes old bonds 'risky', 'volatile' or 'obscure'; none of these would explain why their prices go up. 'Attractive' is correct, so a replacement would spoil the sentence.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (4) may be wrongly used: 'This is why bond prices and interest rates are said to be directly related'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: 'This is why' sums up the two examples
solution.explanation: Paragraph 2 shows that when rates rise, prices fall, and when rates fall, prices rise. Two quantities that move in opposite directions are inversely related.
steps: Rates up → prices down; rates down → prices up
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Closely' and 'loosely' describe how strong the link is, not its direction, so they miss the opposite movement the paragraph has just shown. 'Directly' says they move together, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In the passage, the word in bold numbered (5) may be wrongly used: 'a sharp rise in interest rates can reduce the value of these holdings and strengthen their balance sheets'. Choose the word that should replace it to make the sentence grammatically correct and meaningful. If the word is correct as it stands, choose 'No replacement required'.

solution.concept: Error-based cloze: a loss in the value of assets harms the balance sheet
solution.explanation: When rates rise, the bonds that banks hold lose value. Losing value on assets weakens a balance sheet; it cannot strengthen it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Diversify' and 'publish' have no link with a fall in the value of holdings. 'Strengthen' contradicts 'reduce the value', so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new bank and it's customers (A) / have both benefited (B) / from the faster software. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The new bank and it's customers

solution.concept: 'Its' (possessive: belonging to it) vs 'it's' (short for 'it is' or 'it has')
solution.explanation: The customers belong to the bank, so the possessive 'its' is needed: 'The new bank and its customers have both benefited ...'. 'It's' means 'it is' or 'it has', which makes no sense here.
steps: Test: 'The new bank and it is customers' is meaningless
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B's plural verb agrees with the compound subject 'the bank and its customers'. Part C is correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The new bank and it's customers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
All the money changers at the airport (A) / must comply to (B) / the new rules on foreign currency. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: All the money changers at the airport
the new rules on foreign currency.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'comply with' (a rule, order or request)
solution.explanation: The verb 'comply' takes 'with': 'must comply with the new rules on foreign currency'.
steps: 'comply to' → 'comply with': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct plural subject. Part C is a correct object phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Most of customers (A) / who visited the branch today (B) / came to update their passbooks. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Most' + noun in general ('most customers'), or 'most of' + a determiner + noun ('most of the customers')
solution.explanation: 'Of' after 'most' needs a determiner such as 'the', 'these' or 'our' before the noun: 'Most of the customers who visited the branch today ...' (or simply 'Most customers ...').
steps: 'most of' must be followed by the/these/my etc.
Correct: 'Most of the customers': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct relative clause. Part C ('came to update their passbooks') is correct. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The new clerk don't know (A) / how to use (B) / the note-counting machine yet. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: A third-person singular subject takes 'does', not 'do', in negatives and questions
solution.explanation: 'The new clerk' is third person singular, so the auxiliary must be 'does': 'The new clerk doesn't (does not) know how to use the note-counting machine yet.'
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B ('how to use') is a correct infinitive phrase. Part C correctly places 'yet' at the end of a negative sentence. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The new clerk don't know

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The guard switched off the lights (A) / and locked the main door (B) / before going home. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The guard switched off the lights

solution.concept: Phrasal verb 'switch off', parallel past verbs, and preposition + gerund
solution.explanation: 'Switched off the lights and locked the main door' joins two past-tense verbs with 'and'. 'Before going home' correctly uses a gerund after the preposition 'before'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. Changing C to 'before go home' or B to 'lock' would create an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
This criteria was used (A) / to select the branches (B) / for the new pilot scheme. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Greek-origin plurals: one criterion, two criteria (like phenomenon – phenomena)
solution.explanation: 'Criteria' is the plural of 'criterion'. With 'This' and 'was', a singular is meant: 'This criterion was used ...'. (For the plural: 'These criteria were used ...'.)
steps: 'This criteria' → 'This criterion': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct infinitive of purpose. Part C is a correct prepositional phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: This criteria was used

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The branch manager finally (A) / got the customer sign (B) / the revised loan agreement. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Causative 'get': get + person + to-infinitive (unlike 'make' and 'let', which take a bare infinitive)
solution.explanation: 'Get someone to do something' means persuade them to do it. The 'to' cannot be dropped: 'finally got the customer to sign the revised loan agreement'.
steps: 'got the customer sign' → 'got the customer to sign': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct subject with an adverb. Part C is a correct object. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: got the customer sign

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
My colleague did not attend (A) / the training in Pune, (B) / and so did I. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: Agreeing with a negative statement: 'neither/nor + auxiliary + subject', not 'so + auxiliary + subject'
solution.explanation: 'So did I' agrees with a positive statement ('He attended, and so did I'). After a negative ('did not attend'), agreement is 'and neither did I' (or 'nor did I').
steps: First clause is negative: 'did not attend'
'and so did I' → 'and neither did I': error in part C
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'did not' + base verb. Part B is a correct place phrase. C has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: and so did I.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Visitors are prohibited (A) / to enter the strongroom (B) / without a senior officer. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Prohibit' takes 'from' + -ing: prohibit someone from doing something
solution.explanation: The pattern is 'prohibit + person + from + -ing'; in the passive, 'be prohibited from + -ing': 'Visitors are prohibited from entering the strongroom without a senior officer.'
steps: 'to enter' → 'from entering': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct passive. Part C is a correct phrase. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: to enter the strongroom

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Either of the three cashiers (A) / can open the vault (B) / in the manager's absence. (C) / No error (D)

solution.concept: 'Either' and 'neither' refer to one of two; for three or more, use 'any (one) of' or 'none of'
solution.explanation: 'Either of' is used when there are exactly two. With three cashiers the sentence needs 'Any of the three cashiers can open the vault ...' (or 'Any one of').
steps: 'Either of the three' → 'Any of the three': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B correctly uses the modal 'can' + base verb. Part C is a correct phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Either of the three cashiers

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The two first chapters of the manual (A) / explain the rules (B) / for opening new accounts. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The two first chapters of the manual

solution.concept: Order of numbers: ordinal before cardinal ('the first two', 'the last three'), not 'the two first'
solution.explanation: When an ordinal (first, last, next) and a cardinal (two, three) come together, the ordinal comes first: 'The first two chapters of the manual explain the rules ...'.
steps: 'The two first chapters' → 'The first two chapters': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B's plural verb agrees with 'chapters'. Part C is a correct phrase. A has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The two first chapters of the manual

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
After the firm collapsed, (A) / he not only lost his job (B) / but also his life's savings. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: he not only lost his job

solution.concept: Correlative conjunctions ('not only ... but also') must be followed by the same kind of element
solution.explanation: 'But also' is followed by a noun phrase ('his life's savings'), so 'not only' must be too: 'he lost not only his job but also his life's savings'. As written, 'not only' comes before the verb 'lost' while 'but also' comes before a noun, which breaks the parallel.
steps: 'not only lost his job' → 'lost not only his job': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A is a correct time clause. Part C is the correct second half of the pair; the faulty placement is in B. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option B: he not only lost his job

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
The village where the bank's founder (A) / was born in (B) / now has a branch of its own. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: The village where the bank's founder
now has a branch of its own.

solution.concept: A relative adverb ('where', 'when') already contains the preposition; 'where ... in' repeats it
solution.explanation: 'Where' means 'in which', so adding 'in' at the end of the clause says 'in' twice. Correct: 'The village where the bank's founder was born now has a branch of its own' (or 'The village in which ... was born', or 'The village that ... was born in').
steps: 'where ... was born in' repeats the preposition
Drop 'in': 'was born': error in part B
solution.why_others_wrong: Part A correctly uses 'where' for a place. Part C's singular verb 'has' agrees with 'The village'. B has an error, so 'No error' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
I clearly remember to lock (A) / the vault last night, (B) / so the key must be in the drawer. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: so the key must be in the drawer.

solution.concept: 'Remember + -ing' (recall a past action) vs 'remember + to-infinitive' (not forget a duty)
solution.explanation: The speaker is recalling an action already done 'last night', which needs 'remember + -ing': 'I clearly remember locking the vault last night'. 'Remember to lock' means not forgetting to do it in the future.
steps: 'last night' → the action is in the past
'remember to lock' → 'remember locking': error in part A
solution.why_others_wrong: Part B is a correct object and time phrase. Part C correctly uses 'must be' for a deduction about the present. A has an error of meaning, so 'No error' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: I clearly remember to lock

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Read the sentence to find out whether there is any grammatical or idiomatic error in it. The error, if any, will be in one part of the sentence. Choose that part as the answer. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Were the bank to raise its lending rate again, (A) / many small borrowers (B) / would find it hard to repay. (C) / No error (D)

options.text: Were the bank to raise its lending rate again,
would find it hard to repay.

solution.concept: Inverted conditional with 'Were + subject + to-infinitive' (= If the bank were to raise ...)
solution.explanation: 'Were the bank to raise' is the formal, inverted form of 'If the bank were to raise', used for an unlikely future event. The main clause correctly uses 'would + base verb'.
steps: Part A: inversion with 'Were ... to': correct
Part C: 'would find' for the hypothetical result: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: A, B and C are each correct as shown in the steps. 'Was the bank to raise' or 'will find' would create an error.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
After the twelve-hour audit, the cashier did not **feel like to cook** dinner.

solution.concept: 'Feel like' (= want) is followed by a noun or a gerund
solution.explanation: 'Like' in 'feel like' is a preposition, so the verb after it takes the -ing form: 'the cashier did not feel like cooking dinner'.
steps: 'feel like' = want, be in the mood for
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Feel to cook' drops 'like' and changes the meaning. 'Feel like cook' uses a base verb after a preposition. The original uses a to-infinitive after 'like', so 'No improvement required' is wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
You **need not bring** your passbook yesterday; the bank had already updated your entries online.

solution.concept: 'Need not have + past participle' for something done in the past that turned out to be unnecessary
solution.explanation: The customer brought the passbook yesterday, but it was not needed because the entries were already updated. A past action that was unnecessary is expressed by 'need not have + past participle': 'You need not have brought your passbook yesterday'.
steps: The action happened but was unnecessary
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Must not have brought' is a deduction that he did not bring it, which changes the meaning. 'Did not need bringing' is ungrammatical with a person as subject. 'Need not bring' refers to the present or future, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option C: need not have brought

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
The committee has recommended **that the scheme be extended** to all rural branches.

options.text: that the scheme to be extended

solution.concept: Mandative subjunctive: verbs like recommend, insist and demand + 'that' + subject + base form (or 'should' + base form)
solution.explanation: After 'recommend that', the verb in the 'that' clause takes the base form: 'that the scheme be extended'. 'That the scheme should be extended' would also be correct, but the sentence as written is already correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'That the scheme to be extended' has no finite verb. 'Should extended' drops 'be'. 'Be extend' uses the base form instead of the participle.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following phrases should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically correct? If the sentence is correct as it is, choose 'No improvement required'.
Fifteen tonnes of grain was **a too heavy load** for the old lorry to carry up the hill.

solution.concept: Word order with 'too/so/as/how' + adjective + a/an + noun
solution.explanation: When 'too' (or 'so', 'as', 'how') qualifies an adjective before a singular noun, the order is too + adjective + a + noun: 'too heavy a load'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A so heavy load' uses the wrong order with 'so' ('so heavy a load' would be needed). 'Too much heavy' is wrong because 'much' does not qualify a plain adjective. The original 'a too heavy load' has the wrong order, so 'No improvement required' is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: too heavy a load

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The ATM near the market **ran away of** cash by noon on the day before the festival.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'run': run out of = use up all of something
solution.explanation: When a machine has no cash left, it has 'run out of' cash: 'The ATM ... ran out of cash by noon'.
steps: Meaning needed: had no cash left
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Ran into' means met by chance or collided with. 'Ran off with' means stole and escaped. The original 'ran away of' is not a phrasal verb, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The bank has **set up** a help desk in the village to explain the new pension scheme.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'set': set up = establish, arrange
solution.explanation: To 'set up' a help desk is to establish it. The sentence is correct.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Set off' means start a journey or trigger something. 'Set aside' means keep for later use. 'Set back' means delay. None means established.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
