Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
Please **bear on** me for a few minutes while I check your loan file.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: bear with (someone) = be patient with someone
solution.explanation: The speaker asks the customer to be patient while he checks the file. The phrasal verb for this is 'bear with': 'Please bear with me for a few minutes'.
steps: Meaning needed: be patient with me
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Bear up' means stay cheerful in difficulty. 'Bear out' means confirm (as in 'the facts bear out his claim'). 'Bear on' means relate to and does not take a person in this sense, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Which of the following should replace the phrase in bold to make the sentence grammatically and contextually correct? If no replacement is needed, choose 'No replacement required'.
The union and the management have been **on loggerheads** over the new transfer policy for months.

solution.concept: Fixed expression: 'at loggerheads (with someone / over something)' = in strong disagreement
solution.explanation: Two sides in a long, bitter disagreement are 'at loggerheads'. The fixed expression always takes 'at'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In loggerheads' and 'under loggerheads' are not idiomatic. The original 'on loggerheads' is not the fixed form, so 'No replacement required' does not apply.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: This is the most worst flood the town has seen.
His handwriting is badder than his brother's.
The second road is more worse than the first.
This year's harvest was worse than last year's.

solution.concept: Irregular comparison: bad – worse – worst (never 'more worse', 'most worst' or 'badder')
solution.explanation: 'Bad' has irregular forms: 'worse' (comparative) and 'worst' (superlative). 'This year's harvest was worse than last year's' uses the comparative correctly.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three add 'more' or 'most' to a form that is already comparative or superlative, or invent the regular form 'badder'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: This year's harvest was worse than last year's.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: He always reaches the branch before nine.
She comes always late to the Monday meeting.
They are usually busy on the first of the month.
We have never missed a monthly deadline.

solution.concept: Position of frequency adverbs (always, usually, never): before the main verb, after 'be' and after the first auxiliary
solution.explanation: Frequency adverbs go before a main verb: 'She always comes late to the Monday meeting.' 'Comes always' puts the adverb after the main verb, which is wrong.
steps: 'always reaches': before the main verb: correct
'comes always': after the main verb: incorrect
'have never missed': after the auxiliary: correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three place the adverb correctly: before a main verb, after 'be', or after an auxiliary.
solution.final_answer: Option B: She comes always late to the Monday meeting.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: The meeting is in Monday at ten in the morning.
The meeting is on Monday in ten in the morning.
The meeting is at Monday on ten in the morning.
The meeting is on Monday at ten in the morning.

solution.concept: Prepositions of time: 'on' + day or date, 'at' + clock time, 'in' + part of the day, month or year
solution.explanation: Days take 'on' ('on Monday'), clock times take 'at' ('at ten') and parts of the day take 'in' ('in the morning'). Only one option uses all three correctly.
steps: Part of the day → in the morning
solution.why_others_wrong: The others use 'in Monday', 'at Monday', 'on ten' or 'in ten', each of which breaks the rule for days or clock times.
solution.final_answer: Option D: The meeting is on Monday at ten in the morning.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: Ramesh is a friend of me from college.
Ramesh is a my friend from college.
Ramesh is one my friend from college.
Ramesh is a friend of mine from college.

solution.concept: Double possessive: a/an/this + noun + of + possessive pronoun (a friend of mine, a colleague of hers)
solution.explanation: 'A' and 'my' cannot stand together before a noun. To say 'one of my friends' with 'a', English uses 'a friend of mine', with the possessive pronoun 'mine'.
steps: 'a friend of me' → object pronoun is wrong here
solution.why_others_wrong: The others use the object pronoun 'me', put 'a' and 'my' together, or drop the 'of' that 'one of my friends' needs.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Ramesh is a friend of mine from college.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: The lady has two step-daughters and a son.
Both her sons-in-law work in the same bank.
The commanders-in-chief of the three services met today.
Two passer-bys stopped to help the injured guard.

solution.concept: Plural of compound nouns: the main noun takes the plural (passers-by, sons-in-law, commanders-in-chief)
solution.explanation: In a compound such as 'passer-by', the main word is 'passer' (the person), so it takes the '-s': 'passers-by'. 'Passer-bys' puts the plural on the wrong part.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three put the plural on the main noun of the compound, which is correct.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Two passer-bys stopped to help the injured guard.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct?

options.text: He went to the bank for withdrawing some cash.
He went to the bank for to withdraw some cash.
He went to the bank to withdraw some cash.
He went to the bank for withdraw some cash.

solution.concept: Purpose of a person's action: to-infinitive (not 'for + -ing')
solution.explanation: To say why someone did something, English uses the to-infinitive: 'He went to the bank to withdraw some cash.' 'For + -ing' describes what a thing is used for ('a machine for counting notes'), not a person's purpose.
steps: Purpose of going to the bank → to-infinitive
'for withdrawing' describes a tool's use, not a purpose
solution.why_others_wrong: The others use 'for + -ing', 'for to' or 'for' + base verb, none of which expresses a person's purpose.
solution.final_answer: Option C: He went to the bank to withdraw some cash.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following sentences is grammatically INCORRECT?

options.text: The accident was happened near the toll plaza.
The meeting was postponed because of the strike.
The new branch was opened by the local MLA.
The parcel was delivered to the wrong address.

solution.concept: Intransitive verbs (happen, occur, arrive, die) have no object and therefore no passive form
solution.explanation: 'Happen' cannot take an object, so it cannot be made passive. The correct sentence is 'The accident happened near the toll plaza.'
steps: 'was happened': passive of an intransitive verb: incorrect
solution.why_others_wrong: Postpone, open and deliver are transitive verbs, so their passives are correct.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The accident was happened near the toll plaza.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Every night, after his last trip, he sat under the streetlight near the depot with his books.
(B) Suresh worked as a conductor on a city bus, but he dreamt of becoming a teacher.
(C) Last month, the former conductor of route 21 took charge of his first class.
(D) His regular passengers soon noticed and began lending him their old guidebooks.
(E) Three years later, he passed the teachers' eligibility test on his second attempt.

solution.concept: Para jumble: named opener, then time order (dream → effort → help → success → result)
solution.explanation: B introduces Suresh and his dream. A ('he', 'every night') shows his effort. D ('noticed') refers to his studying under the streetlight. E ('Three years later') gives the exam result, and C ('Last month') the present outcome.
steps: A → D: passengers notice the study
D → E → C: exam passed, then his first class: BADEC
solution.why_others_wrong: BDAEC has passengers 'notice' before there is anything to notice. ABDEC opens with 'he' before Suresh is named. BAEDC has passengers lend guidebooks after he has already passed the test.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Every morning at eight, two students of a village school read the rain gauge in the playground.
(P) They then chalk the figure on a board beside the school gate.
(Q) Encouraged by this interest, the school now keeps ten years of readings in a register that anyone may consult.
(R) Farmers passing by soon began to check the board before deciding when to sow.
(S) A few of them even come back in the evening to ask how much rain fell in the same week last year.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'They then', 'the board', 'A few of them' and 'this interest' as links
solution.explanation: P ('They then') continues the students' routine. R ('the board') tells how farmers use the board. S ('A few of them') refers to the farmers. Q ('this interest') sums up the farmers' interest and gives the school's response.
steps: R → S: 'A few of them' = farmers
S → Q: 'this interest' leads to the register: PRSQ
solution.why_others_wrong: PSRQ uses 'A few of them' before the farmers are mentioned. RPSQ has farmers check 'the board' before it is introduced. PRQS gives the school's response before the evening visits that show the interest.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) For two years the plants bore nothing, and even Raghu began to have doubts.
(B) Today, several of the neighbours who once laughed buy saplings from him.
(C) Neighbours laughed when Raghu pulled out his cotton plants and set up concrete poles across his field.
(D) In the third summer, however, the poles were heavy with bright pink fruit.
(E) The poles, he explained, were to support dragon fruit, a cactus that needs little water.

solution.concept: Para jumble: setting → explanation → setback → turning point ('however') → present result
solution.explanation: C introduces Raghu and the strange poles. E ('The poles, he explained') explains them. A gives the two barren years. D ('In the third summer, however') is the turning point. B ('Today') gives the result.
steps: E → A: two years with no fruit
A → D ('however', third summer) → B ('Today'): CEADB
solution.why_others_wrong: CAEDB mentions 'the plants' before E says what was planted. ECADB opens with 'he' and 'The poles' before Raghu is introduced. CEDAB puts the third-summer harvest before the first two barren years.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Over time, only the debased coins remained in circulation.
(B) In the past, coins were made of gold or silver, and their value depended on the metal they contained.
(C) People naturally spent the debased coins and hoarded the full-weight ones.
(D) When a ruler issued new coins with less precious metal but the same face value as the old ones, the two kinds circulated side by side.
(E) This tendency, summed up as 'bad money drives out good', is known as Gresham's law.

solution.concept: Para jumble: background → event → behaviour → result → name of the principle ('This tendency')
solution.explanation: B gives the background (value from metal). D describes the debasement and two kinds of coin. C ('the debased coins') gives people's behaviour. A ('Over time') states the result. E ('This tendency') names it.
steps: D → C: people spend bad, hoard good
C → A ('Over time') → E ('This tendency'): BDCAE
solution.why_others_wrong: BCDAE mentions 'the debased coins' before D introduces them. DBCAE opens with an event before the background that explains why less metal matters. BDACE gives the result before the behaviour that causes it.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) When enough people in a community are vaccinated against a contagious disease, even those who are not vaccinated gain some protection.
(P) A newborn baby or a patient undergoing cancer treatment, for instance, may be unable to take certain vaccines.
(Q) This is because the infection finds too few unprotected people to pass through, and its spread slows or stops.
(R) Such protection matters most for people who cannot be vaccinated themselves.
(S) Their safety therefore depends on the choices made by those around them.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'This is because', 'Such protection', 'for instance' and 'Their safety' as links
solution.explanation: Q ('This is because') explains the protection in (1). R ('Such protection') says who needs it most. P ('for instance') gives examples of such people. S ('Their safety') concludes about them.
steps: (1) → Q: the reason for the protection
Q → R: 'Such protection' matters most for some
solution.why_others_wrong: QPRS gives examples before saying what they are examples of. RPQS separates 'This is because' from the claim in (1) that it explains. QRSP uses 'Their' before the people it refers to have been described.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) Engineers solve the problem by leaving small gaps, called expansion joints, at regular intervals along the structure.
(B) If a long concrete bridge were built as one solid piece, this movement would set up huge stresses.
(C) Like most materials, concrete expands slightly in summer heat and contracts in winter cold.
(D) Over time, these stresses could crack the deck or push the supports out of line.
(E) Drivers often feel these joints as a gentle bump at regular points on a flyover.

solution.concept: Para jumble: fact → problem ('this movement') → consequence ('these stresses') → solution → everyday sign
solution.explanation: C states the fact of expansion. B ('this movement') shows the problem it causes. D ('these stresses') gives the damage. A ('the problem') gives the solution. E ('these joints') links it to everyday experience.
steps: C → B: 'this movement' = expansion and contraction
D → A ('the problem') → E ('these joints'): CBDAE
solution.why_others_wrong: CDBAE mentions 'these stresses' before any stress is introduced. BCDAE opens with 'this movement' before the movement is described. CBADE solves the problem before its consequences are stated and leaves 'these stresses' after the solution.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) In many villages, a common pasture is open to every family's cattle.
(P) Each family therefore has a reason to add one more animal, even when the land is already overgrazed.
(Q) The cost of the damage to the grass, by contrast, is shared among all the families.
(R) The benefit of grazing an extra cow, however, goes wholly to the family that owns it.
(S) When every family reasons in this way, the pasture is ruined for all.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'however', 'by contrast', 'therefore' and 'in this way' as links
solution.explanation: R ('however') contrasts the shared pasture with a private benefit. Q ('by contrast') sets the shared cost against that benefit. P ('therefore') draws the family's conclusion. S ('in this way') shows the result when all do it.
steps: (1) → R: shared land, but private benefit
R → Q: 'by contrast', the cost is shared
Q → P: 'therefore' each family adds an animal
solution.why_others_wrong: QRPS states the cost 'by contrast' before the benefit it is contrasted with. RPQS draws the conclusion ('therefore') before the shared cost that completes the reason. PRQS starts with 'therefore' before any reason is given.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following five sentences (A), (B), (C), (D) and (E) to form a meaningful paragraph. Then choose the correct order.
(A) To prevent such a spiral, stock exchanges use circuit breakers.
(B) When prices fall sharply, frightened investors often rush to sell, pushing prices down even further.
(C) These rules halt trading for a fixed period once an index falls by a set percentage in a day.
(D) The pause gives investors time to absorb the news and think before they act.
(E) Critics argue, however, that the prospect of a halt can itself cause panic, as traders hurry to sell before the market closes.

solution.concept: Para jumble: problem → solution ('such a spiral') → how it works ('These rules') → benefit ('The pause') → criticism ('however')
solution.explanation: B describes the falling spiral. A ('such a spiral') introduces circuit breakers. C ('These rules') explains them. D ('The pause') gives the benefit. E ('however') gives the critics' view.
solution.why_others_wrong: BCADE uses 'These rules' before any rule is named. ABCDE opens with 'such a spiral' before the spiral is described. BADCE mentions 'The pause' before C explains that trading is halted.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Sentence (1) is fixed as the first sentence. Rearrange sentences P, Q, R and S that follow it to form a meaningful paragraph, and choose the correct order.
(1) Suppose a skilled lawyer can also type faster than her assistant.
(P) Every hour she spends typing is an hour taken away from legal work that earns far more.
(Q) Even so, it makes sense for her to leave the typing to the assistant.
(R) Economists use the same reasoning, called comparative advantage, to explain why countries trade.
(S) Both of them gain when each concentrates on the work at which they are relatively better.

solution.concept: Fixed opener; 'Even so', the reason, the conclusion about 'both of them', then the general principle
solution.explanation: Q ('Even so') gives the surprising conclusion despite (1). P explains why: her time is worth more at legal work. S ('Both of them') states the gain for lawyer and assistant. R ('the same reasoning') extends it to countries.
steps: Q → P: the reason (cost of her hour)
S → R: 'the same reasoning' for countries: QPSR
solution.why_others_wrong: PQSR separates 'Even so' from the fact in (1) that it answers. QSPR states the shared gain before the reason for the arrangement. QPRS extends the reasoning to countries before finishing the lawyer's case.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) did not
(Q) the customer
(R) sign the cheque
(S) because he had forgotten his glasses

solution.concept: Subject + auxiliary + 'not' + base verb + object, then the reason clause
solution.explanation: 'The customer did not sign the cheque because he had forgotten his glasses.' Subject (Q), negative auxiliary (P), base verb + object (R), reason (S).
steps: Verb + object: R; reason: S → QPRS
solution.why_others_wrong: QRPS puts the verb before 'did not'. PQSR opens with 'did not' before any subject. RQPS opens with a verb phrase.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) than the lights went out
(Q) no sooner had
(R) begun his speech
(S) the chairman

solution.concept: Inversion after 'No sooner': 'No sooner had + subject + past participle ... than ...'
solution.explanation: 'No sooner had the chairman begun his speech than the lights went out.' 'No sooner had' (Q) is followed by the subject (S) and the participle (R); the 'than' clause (P) comes last.
solution.why_others_wrong: SQRP puts the subject before 'No sooner had'. QRSP puts the participle before the subject. QSPR puts the 'than' clause before the chairman has begun anything.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) the small firm would have
(Q) were it not for
(R) lost its biggest contract
(S) the bank's timely loan

solution.concept: Inverted conditional: 'Were it not for + noun, ... would have + past participle'
solution.explanation: 'Were it not for the bank's timely loan, the small firm would have lost its biggest contract.' 'Were it not for' (Q) takes a noun phrase (S); the main clause follows (P + R).
steps: Condition: Q + S ('Were it not for the bank's timely loan')
Main clause: P ('the small firm would have')
solution.why_others_wrong: QPSR puts the main clause between 'Were it not for' and its noun. SQPR opens with a noun phrase that has no verb. QSRP puts 'lost its biggest contract' before its subject and auxiliary.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Rearrange the following parts (P), (Q), (R) and (S) to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
(P) as to approve
(Q) have the directors been so willing
(R) rarely
(S) a loan without any collateral

solution.concept: Inversion after 'Rarely' (auxiliary before subject) + 'so ... as to + infinitive'
solution.explanation: 'Rarely have the directors been so willing as to approve a loan without any collateral.' 'Rarely' (R) needs inversion (Q); 'so willing' is completed by 'as to approve' (P), whose object follows (S).
steps: Inverted clause: Q ('have the directors been so willing')
'so ... as to' + verb: P; object: S → RQPS
solution.why_others_wrong: QRPS places 'rarely' in the middle, where the inversion has no trigger. RPQS puts 'as to approve' before 'so willing'. RQSP separates 'as to approve' from 'so willing' and leaves it without an object.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The lecture on tax rules was so ______ that half the trainees were yawning within ten minutes.

solution.concept: Single blank: the 'so ... that' result decides the word
solution.explanation: Trainees yawning within ten minutes shows the lecture was dull and tiring: 'tedious'.
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'lively' or 'useful' lecture would not make people yawn. 'Brief' does not explain yawning within ten minutes.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The old cashier's honesty is beyond ______; in forty years, not a single rupee has gone missing at his counter.

solution.concept: Fixed phrase: beyond reproach = so good that no one could find fault
solution.explanation: Forty years without a rupee going missing shows that no one can find fault with his honesty: it is 'beyond reproach'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Beyond repair' means too damaged to fix. 'Beyond reach' means out of reach. 'Beyond return' is not an idiom. None describes faultless honesty.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The ______ of the new bridge has been delayed because the contractor has not yet ______ the steel.

solution.concept: Double blank: a delay caused by a missing material
solution.explanation: Building (construction) cannot go on without steel. The delay is explained by steel that has not yet arrived: 'has not yet received the steel'.
steps: Blank 1: a new bridge is being built → construction
Blank 2: the steel has not arrived → received
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Destruction' makes no sense for a new bridge. 'Has not yet refused the steel' gives no reason for delay. 'Opening' and 'returned' do not link the delay to missing steel.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
Volunteers were asked to ______ the leaflets about the free health camp to every house in the lane.

solution.concept: Phrasal verbs with 'hand': hand out = distribute to many people
solution.explanation: Giving a leaflet to every house in the lane is distributing it: 'hand out the leaflets'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Hand down' means pass to a younger generation. 'Hand in' means submit to an authority. 'Hand back' means return. None means distribute.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The new penalty rules are ______: they apply only to loans taken after 1 April, not to older ones.

solution.concept: Prospective (applying to the future) vs retrospective (applying to the past)
solution.explanation: Rules that apply only from a date onwards, and not to earlier loans, take effect for the future: they are 'prospective'.
steps: Clue: only loans taken after 1 April
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Retrospective' is the opposite (applying to the past). 'Perspective' is a noun meaning point of view. 'Provisional' (temporary) does not match the explanation after the colon.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
When reporters asked about the missing funds, the official remained ______, saying only that an inquiry was under way.

solution.concept: Single blank: the participle phrase defines the word
solution.explanation: Saying 'only that an inquiry was under way' means refusing to give details: being 'tight-lipped'.
steps: Meaning needed: unwilling to say much
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Outspoken' and 'long-winded' describe someone who says a lot. 'Light-hearted' (cheerful) does not fit a refusal to talk about missing funds.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The ______ rise in onion prices, which doubled in a fortnight, ______ the government to ban exports.

solution.concept: Double blank: a relative clause defines the first word; the result decides the second
solution.explanation: Prices that double in a fortnight show a 'steep' rise. A steep rise would push (prompt) the government to act by banning exports.
steps: Blank 1: doubled in a fortnight → steep
Blank 2: led the government to act → prompted
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Gradual' and 'modest' contradict doubling in a fortnight. 'Prevented the government to ban' is both illogical and ungrammatical ('prevent from').

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
Although the inquiry ______ the manager of any wrongdoing, the ______ of the scandal stayed with him for years.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'Although' sets an official result against a lasting effect
solution.explanation: 'Clear someone of wrongdoing' means declare them innocent. 'Although' introduces a contrast: even so, the shame or 'stigma' of the scandal stayed with him.
steps: Blank 1: '___ him of any wrongdoing' → cleared
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Accused of wrongdoing' removes the contrast with a lasting stigma. 'Glory' does not come from a scandal. 'Convicted ... shame' removes the contrast that 'Although' requires.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The new disclosure rules are expected to ______ the practice of hiding fees in the fine print.

solution.concept: Phrase meaning: put an end to = stop completely
solution.explanation: Disclosure rules are meant to stop a bad practice. 'Put an end to' means stop it.
steps: Purpose of disclosure rules: stop it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Make way for' means allow something to replace you. 'Come up with' means think of. 'Fall in with' means agree to. None means stop.
solution.final_answer: Option B: put an end to

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The minister's ______ reply, a single sentence that answered none of the questions, angered the opposition benches.

solution.concept: Single blank: the appositive ('a single sentence that answered none of the questions') defines the word
solution.explanation: A reply of one sentence that answers nothing and angers listeners is rudely short: 'curt'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Effusive' (gushing) and 'exhaustive' (complete) contradict 'a single sentence'. 'Eloquent' (fluent and persuasive) would not anger listeners by answering nothing.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
Far from being ______, the cost overrun was the predictable result of years of poor planning.

solution.concept: Single blank: 'Far from being X' denies X; the rest of the sentence states the opposite
solution.explanation: The sentence says the overrun was 'predictable'. 'Far from being' must therefore deny the opposite quality: it was far from being 'unforeseeable'.
steps: 'Far from being X' = not at all X
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Avoidable' contradicts the point: a result of poor planning could have been avoided. 'Deliberate' and 'negligible' are not opposites of 'predictable', so 'far from being' would not set up the contrast.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
The committee's report ______ the bank's management for its weak controls but stopped short of ______ any individual officer.

solution.concept: Double blank: 'but stopped short of' marks a step that was not taken
solution.explanation: A report on weak controls criticises the management: it 'censured' them. 'Stopped short of' means it did not go further, that is, it did not name any officer.
steps: 'stopped short of' = did not go as far as
Blank 2: the further step = naming individuals
solution.why_others_wrong: Reports do not 'praise' weak controls. 'Stopped short of praising' is not a further step after censure. 'Exonerated' (cleared) clashes with 'weak controls'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the pair of words that best fills the blanks.
A ______ of cheap credit, kept going for too long, can ______ asset bubbles that end in painful crashes.

solution.concept: Double blank: cause (plenty of credit) and effect (bubbles) must match
solution.explanation: Bubbles grow when money is plentiful. A 'glut' (excess) of cheap credit can 'inflate' (blow up) asset bubbles.
steps: Cheap credit kept going too long → an excess (glut)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Dearth' and 'shortage' mean too little credit, which does not create bubbles. 'Deflate' bubbles contradicts 'end in painful crashes'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
When the auditors began asking awkward questions, the finance head tried to ______ by blaming a junior clerk.

solution.concept: Idiomatic phrase: pass the buck = shift responsibility onto someone else
solution.explanation: Blaming a junior clerk to avoid answering the auditors is shifting the responsibility: 'pass the buck'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Steal the show' means attract the most attention. 'Toe the line' means obey the rules. 'Bite the dust' means fail or die. None means shifting blame.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the phrase that best fills the blank.
The two banks' merger plans have been put ______ since the regulator raised objections to the deal.

solution.concept: Idiomatic phrase: on the back burner = set aside for later, given low priority
solution.explanation: After the regulator's objections, the plans are not being pursued for now: they have been 'put on the back burner'.
steps: Effect: the plans are set aside
solution.why_others_wrong: 'In the pipeline' and 'in the offing' mean about to happen, the opposite of being shelved. 'Above board' means honest and open. Also, only 'on the back burner' fits after 'put'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: on the back burner

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'quiet' used correctly?

options.text: The new branch is quiet close to the bus stand.
She has quiet a lot of work this week.
The banking hall was quiet after the lunch rush.
The loan amount was quiet large for a farmer.

solution.concept: Quiet (adjective: making little noise) vs quite (adverb: fairly, completely)
solution.explanation: 'Quiet' means making little noise. A banking hall after the lunch rush has few people and little noise.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three need the adverb 'quite' (fairly, rather) before an adjective or 'a lot'.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The banking hall was quiet after the lunch rush.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
The **(A) premium** paid the **(B) policyholder** on time, so the **(C) insurer** settled the **(D) claim** quickly.

solution.concept: Word swap: check who can perform each action
solution.explanation: A policyholder pays a premium; a premium cannot pay anyone. Swapping A and B gives: 'The policyholder paid the premium on time, so the insurer settled the claim quickly.'
steps: 'The premium paid the policyholder' is meaningless
The rest fits: the insurer settles the claim
solution.why_others_wrong: C-D gives 'the claim settled the insurer'. B-C gives 'The premium paid the insurer ... the policyholder settled the claim', which still has a premium paying someone. The sentence clearly needs a swap.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'mitigate' used correctly?

options.text: The high fees will mitigate against small investors joining the scheme.
Planting trees along the river helped to mitigate the damage from floods.
The two brothers decided to mitigate their dispute in court.
She tried to mitigate her friend into lending her the money.

solution.concept: Mitigate (make less severe) vs militate (against) (work against, make less likely)
solution.explanation: To 'mitigate' damage is to make it less severe. Trees along a river reduce flood damage, so they help to mitigate it.
steps: 'mitigate their dispute in court' → 'litigate' (go to court)
solution.why_others_wrong: The first confuses 'mitigate' with 'militate'. The third confuses it with 'litigate'. The fourth uses it as if it meant 'persuade'.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Planting trees along the river helped to mitigate the damage from floods.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'venal' used correctly?

options.text: The doctor said the cut was venal and would heal in a week.
He made a venal error in the ledger, which was easily corrected.
The venal officer would approve any file for a suitable bribe.
Her venal face showed how little she had slept.

solution.concept: Venal (open to bribery, corrupt) vs venial (minor, pardonable) vs venous (of the veins)
solution.explanation: 'Venal' describes a person who can be bribed. An officer who approves any file for a bribe is venal.
steps: A minor cut → not 'venal' (it has nothing to do with bribery)
An officer open to bribes → 'venal': correct
solution.why_others_wrong: The second confuses 'venal' with 'venial' (pardonable). The first and fourth use it for things that have nothing to do with corruption.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The venal officer would approve any file for a suitable bribe.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: In which of the following sentences is the word 'infer' used correctly?

options.text: Are you inferring that I took the money from the drawer?
His tone inferred that he was unhappy with the decision.
The report infers that the bank's losses will rise next year.
From his silence, the manager inferred that the clerk knew more.

solution.concept: Infer (the listener draws a conclusion) vs imply (the speaker or evidence suggests something)
solution.explanation: To 'infer' is to reach a conclusion from evidence. The manager drew a conclusion from the clerk's silence, so he 'inferred' it.
solution.why_others_wrong: In the other three, the subject (a speaker, a report, a tone) suggests something, which is 'imply', not 'infer'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: From his silence, the manager inferred that the clerk knew more.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
In the sentence below, four words are in bold. Two of them may need to be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful. Choose the correct swap; if no swap is needed, choose 'No swap required'.
Higher **(A) interest rates** make **(B) borrowing** costlier and **(C) saving** more **(D) attractive**.

solution.concept: Word swap: test each bold word in its slot using economic logic
solution.explanation: When interest rates rise, loans cost more (borrowing becomes costlier) and deposits earn more (saving becomes more attractive). Every word fits its place.
steps: Higher rates → loans cost more: 'borrowing costlier'
Higher rates → deposits earn more: 'saving more attractive'
solution.why_others_wrong: B-C gives 'make saving costlier and borrowing more attractive', which reverses the effect of higher rates. A-B and A-D produce nonsense ('Higher borrowing make interest rates costlier').

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'levy' as used in the sentence:
'The bank will levy a small charge on every cash deposit above ten lakh rupees in a month.'

solution.concept: Levy (verb) = impose a tax, fee or charge
solution.explanation: The bank will put a charge on large cash deposits. To 'levy' a charge is to impose it.
steps: Subject: the bank; object: a small charge
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Waive', 'refund' and 'reduce' all lighten or remove the charge; to levy it is to put it on.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are SIMILAR in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Feeble' and 'weak' both mean lacking strength. The other pairs are opposites.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are opposites, not synonyms.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'inundated' as used in the sentence:
'After the bank announced free locker rents for a year, the branch was inundated with applications.'

solution.concept: Inundated = flooded, overwhelmed (with more than can be handled)
solution.explanation: A popular free offer brings far more applications than usual. The branch was flooded or overwhelmed with them.
steps: Effect: a huge number of applications
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Refused', 'delayed' and 'examined' describe what the branch might do with applications, not the flood of applications arriving.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'anomalies' as used in the sentence:
'The year-end audit brought to light several anomalies in the branch's cash records.'

solution.concept: Anomaly = something that departs from what is normal or expected
solution.explanation: Audits 'bring to light' problems. Entries in cash records that do not fit the normal pattern are irregularities.
steps: Context: an audit 'brought to light' (uncovered) something
Things an audit uncovers: departures from the norm
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Improvements', 'agreements' and 'summaries' are not things an audit uncovers as problems; 'brought to light' suggests something wrong.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Which of the following pairs consists of words that are OPPOSITE in meaning?

solution.concept: Word pairs: identify synonyms and antonyms
solution.explanation: 'Opulent' means very wealthy and luxurious; 'impoverished' means very poor. They are opposites. The other pairs are synonyms.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other three pairs are synonyms, not opposites.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the word 'salutary' as used in the sentence:
'The heavy fine imposed on one careless lender had a salutary effect: the others quickly tightened their checks.'

solution.concept: Salutary = producing a good effect, often through an unpleasant experience
solution.explanation: One lender's fine led the others to improve their checks. The effect was good (beneficial), even though it came from a penalty.
steps: Event: a heavy fine on one lender
Result: others tightened their checks (an improvement)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Harmful' contradicts the improvement that followed. 'Temporary' is not supported. 'Ceremonial' confuses 'salutary' with 'salute'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The new clerk was **courteous** to every customer, even to those who were rude to him.

solution.concept: Courteous = polite and respectful
solution.explanation: Being courteous even to rude customers means being polite and respectful to them.
steps: Context: kind behaviour even to rude people
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Strict', 'nervous' and 'careless' do not describe respectful behaviour towards customers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Lending to small traders has proved surprisingly **lucrative** for the cooperative bank.

solution.concept: Lucrative = producing a lot of money, profitable
solution.explanation: A line of lending that is 'lucrative' brings in good profits.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Risky' and 'tiresome' describe drawbacks. 'Popular' describes demand, not profit.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
Facing heavy losses, the airline **jettisoned** its plan to fly to three new cities.

solution.concept: Jettison = throw away, abandon (a plan or an idea)
solution.explanation: Heavy losses forced the airline to drop its expansion plan altogether: it 'jettisoned' (abandoned) it.
steps: Action on a costly plan: drop it
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Postponed' means delayed, not dropped. 'Announced' and 'expanded' do not fit a company cutting back because of losses.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The audience remained **apathetic** throughout the minister's speech on rural credit.

solution.concept: Apathetic = showing no interest or enthusiasm; antonym: enthusiastic
solution.explanation: An 'apathetic' audience shows no interest. The opposite is an 'enthusiastic' one.
steps: Opposite: full of interest and eagerness
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Indifferent', 'uninterested' and 'listless' are all close in meaning to 'apathetic'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in bold as used in the sentence.
The businessman's **ostentatious** wedding, with its gold-plated invitations, drew wide criticism.

solution.concept: Ostentatious = designed to impress by showing off wealth; antonym: understated
solution.explanation: Gold-plated invitations show a wish to display wealth. The opposite of such a showy event is an 'understated' one, simple and modest in style.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Showy', 'lavish' and 'flamboyant' are all close in meaning to 'ostentatious'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to call it a day'.

options.text: to stop working for the time being
to give a day a special name
to postpone a meeting to the next day

solution.concept: Idiom: call it a day = decide to stop doing something, especially work, for now
solution.explanation: To 'call it a day' is to stop working and go home. For example: 'After clearing the last cheque, the clerks called it a day.'
steps: Image: declaring the day's work over
solution.why_others_wrong: Naming a day and telephoning daily read the words literally. Postponing a meeting is a different idea: the idiom means stopping, not rescheduling.
solution.final_answer: Option A: to stop working for the time being

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
Ravi had agreed to invest in his friend's shop, but he **got cold feet** when he saw the rent agreement.

options.text: became too nervous to go ahead

solution.concept: Idiom: get cold feet = become nervous and withdraw from a plan
solution.explanation: Ravi had agreed to invest, but the rent agreement made him lose his nerve: he 'got cold feet' and hesitated to go ahead.
steps: Context: agreed, then hesitated on seeing the terms
Idiom: lose one's nerve before acting
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Fell ill' takes 'cold feet' literally. 'Lost his temper' and 'got a better offer' are not what the idiom means.
solution.final_answer: Option B: became too nervous to go ahead

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text: Choose the meaning of the idiom 'to steal someone's thunder'.

options.text: to frighten someone with a loud noise
to borrow money without repaying it
to take credit or attention meant for someone else
to make someone lose an argument

solution.concept: Idiom: steal someone's thunder = take the attention or praise that another person expected
solution.explanation: If a colleague announces your idea at a meeting just before you do, he 'steals your thunder': he gets the attention that should have been yours.
steps: Meaning: taking credit or attention meant for another
solution.why_others_wrong: A loud noise reads 'thunder' literally. Unpaid borrowing and losing an argument are not what the idiom means.
solution.final_answer: Option C: to take credit or attention meant for someone else

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the meaning of the idiom in bold.
When three of its largest borrowers defaulted in one quarter, the small lender's owners **saw the writing on the wall** and began looking for a buyer.

options.text: read the terms of the loan agreements carefully
decided to take the defaulters to court
noticed that someone had damaged their office
recognised the signs of coming failure

solution.concept: Idiom: see the writing on the wall = recognise clear signs that something bad, such as failure, is coming
solution.explanation: Three large defaults in one quarter were a clear warning. The owners understood that the business was heading for failure and prepared to sell it.
steps: Context: heavy defaults, then looking for a buyer
Idiom: recognise signs of approaching failure
solution.why_others_wrong: Reading loan terms and damaged walls take the image literally. Going to court is not suggested by 'began looking for a buyer'.
solution.final_answer: Option D: recognised the signs of coming failure

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A place where old public records and historical documents are kept

solution.concept: One-word substitution: places for keeping things
solution.explanation: 'Archives' is the place where historical records and documents are stored.
steps: Key idea: old records and documents
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'museum' displays objects, a 'library' lends books, and a 'gallery' displays works of art.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
The practice of those in power giving jobs or favours to their relatives

solution.concept: One-word substitution: misuse of power
solution.explanation: 'Nepotism' is favouring relatives (from Latin 'nepos', nephew or grandson), especially by giving them jobs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Favouritism' is unfair preference for anyone, not specifically relatives. 'Patronage' is support given by a patron. 'Bribery' is paying someone to act dishonestly.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the one word that can be substituted for the given group of words.
A person who falsely claims to have special knowledge or skill

solution.concept: One-word substitution: types of people
solution.explanation: A 'charlatan' is a fraud who pretends to have knowledge or skill, such as a fake doctor.
steps: Key idea: false claim to expertise
solution.why_others_wrong: A 'connoisseur' is a genuine expert in matters of taste. A 'novice' is a beginner who makes no false claim. A 'sycophant' flatters powerful people.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The bank has issued new debit cards to all its customers.

options.text: New debit cards were issued to all its customers by the bank.
New debit cards have issued to all its customers by the bank.
New debit cards have been issued to all its customers by the bank.
New debit cards had been issued to all its customers by the bank.

solution.concept: Present perfect active (has/have + past participle) → has/have been + past participle
solution.explanation: The object 'new debit cards' becomes the subject. 'Has issued' becomes 'have been issued' (plural subject), and the agent follows 'by'.
steps: Present perfect passive: have been + issued
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Were issued' changes the tense to the simple past. 'Have issued' drops 'been' and is not passive. 'Had been issued' changes the tense to the past perfect.
solution.final_answer: Option C: New debit cards have been issued to all its customers by the bank.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in passive voice.
The engineers were repairing the main server when the power failed.

options.text: The main server was repaired by the engineers when the power failed.
The main server had been repaired by the engineers when the power failed.
The main server was being repaired by the engineers when the power failed.
The main server was repairing by the engineers when the power failed.

solution.concept: Past continuous active (was/were + -ing) → was/were being + past participle
solution.explanation: 'Were repairing' describes an action in progress. Its passive keeps the continuous form: 'was being repaired'. The 'when' clause is not changed.
steps: Past continuous passive: was being + repaired
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was repaired' loses the sense of an action in progress. 'Had been repaired' says the repair was already over. 'Was repairing' is active in form and makes the server the one doing the repair.
solution.final_answer: Option C: The main server was being repaired by the engineers when the power failed.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
The visitor said to me, "May I use your phone for a minute?"

options.text: The visitor asked me if he might use my phone for a minute.
The visitor asked me that may he use my phone for a minute.
The visitor told me if he may use your phone for a minute.
The visitor asked me whether might he use my phone for a minute.

solution.concept: Reported yes/no question with 'may': asked + if/whether + statement order; 'may' → 'might'
solution.explanation: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked (me) if/whether', followed by statement word order. 'May' is backshifted to 'might', 'I' becomes 'he' and 'your' becomes 'my'.
solution.why_others_wrong: The second uses 'that' with question order. The third uses 'told', keeps 'may' and 'your'. The fourth keeps question order ('might he use') after 'whether'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: The visitor asked me if he might use my phone for a minute.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly expresses the given sentence in indirect (reported) speech.
He said to me, "Don't wait for me if I am late."

options.text: He told me not to wait for him if he was late.
He told me to not wait for me if I was late.
He said me not to wait for him if he is late.
He told me that don't wait for him if he was late.

solution.concept: Negative command → told + object + not + to-infinitive; the 'if' clause is backshifted and its pronouns change
solution.explanation: 'Don't wait' becomes 'not to wait' after 'told me'. In the 'if' clause, 'I am' becomes 'he was', and 'for me' becomes 'for him'.
steps: 'for me ... I am late' → 'for him ... he was late'
solution.why_others_wrong: The second keeps 'for me' and 'I'. The third uses 'said me' and keeps 'is'. The fourth keeps the imperative 'don't wait' after 'that'.
solution.final_answer: Option A: He told me not to wait for him if he was late.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
After the bus accident, the injured ______ taken to the district hospital.

solution.concept: 'The + adjective' (the injured, the poor, the elderly) refers to a group of people and takes a plural verb
solution.explanation: 'The injured' means 'the injured people', which is plural. So the verb is plural: 'the injured were taken to the district hospital'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Was' and 'is' are singular. 'Has taken' would be active and make the injured the ones doing the taking.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
What these small borrowers need most ______ timely credit, not another loan waiver.

solution.concept: A 'what' clause used as the subject is normally singular
solution.explanation: The subject is the whole clause 'What these small borrowers need most', which is treated as singular even though it contains the plural noun 'borrowers': 'What these small borrowers need most is timely credit ...'.
steps: Subject: the clause 'What these small borrowers need most'
A clause as subject → singular verb
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Are', 'have been' and 'were' are plural, agreeing wrongly with 'borrowers' inside the clause.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the verb form that correctly fills the blank.
It is I who ______ to blame for the delay in sending the statements.

solution.concept: In 'It is I/you/we who ...', the verb after 'who' agrees with the pronoun before it
solution.explanation: 'Who' refers back to 'I', so the verb takes the form that goes with 'I': 'It is I who am to blame'.
steps: 'It is I who am to blame'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Is' agrees wrongly with 'It'. 'Are' does not agree with 'I'. 'Be' is not a finite form.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
According to the timetable, the first train to Pune ______ at 5.40 tomorrow morning.

solution.concept: Simple present for a future event fixed by a timetable
solution.explanation: Events fixed by an official timetable or schedule take the simple present even when they are in the future: 'the first train to Pune leaves at 5.40 tomorrow morning'.
steps: 'According to the timetable' → a scheduled event
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Left', 'has left' and 'had left' are past or perfect forms that clash with 'tomorrow morning'.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
If I ______ a car, I would drive to the branch every day.

solution.concept: Second conditional: If + simple past, ... would + base verb (an unreal or unlikely present situation)
solution.explanation: The speaker does not have a car; the situation is imagined. The 'if' clause takes the simple past ('had') and the main clause 'would + base verb'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Have' gives a first conditional, which needs 'will drive'. 'Will have' and 'would have' are not used in the 'if' clause here.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
By next March, she ______ at this branch for ten years.

solution.concept: Future perfect continuous: an action continuing up to a point in the future, with its duration
solution.explanation: 'By next March' fixes a future point, and 'for ten years' gives the length of an action continuing up to it. This needs 'will have been working'.
steps: Duration up to that point: 'for ten years'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Will be working' describes an action in progress at a future time but cannot measure duration up to it. 'Has been working' is anchored to now, not to next March. 'Would work' is conditional.
solution.final_answer: Option C: will have been working

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
It was the first time that Mohan ______ a loan, so he read every clause of the agreement twice.

solution.concept: 'It was the first/second time (that) ...' takes the past perfect
solution.explanation: Just as 'It is the first time' takes the present perfect, 'It was the first time' (a past frame) takes the past perfect: 'It was the first time that Mohan had taken a loan'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Has taken' belongs with 'It is the first time'. 'Took' and 'was taking' are not used after 'It was the first time that' in standard grammar.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
Both cashiers at the counter were wearing ______ same blue uniform.

solution.concept: 'The' is always used with 'same'
solution.explanation: 'Same' points to one particular thing that is shared, so it always takes 'the': 'the same blue uniform'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A same' and 'an same' are never used. Without an article, 'wearing same blue uniform' is ungrammatical.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank(s).
What ______ lovely weather we are having! And what ______ beautiful garden the bank has planted!

solution.concept: Exclamations with 'What': 'What a/an + singular countable noun!' but 'What + uncountable or plural noun!'
solution.explanation: 'Weather' is uncountable, so it takes no article: 'What lovely weather!'. 'Garden' is singular and countable, so it takes 'a': 'What a beautiful garden!'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'A lovely weather' treats an uncountable noun as countable. Dropping 'a' before 'beautiful garden' is wrong. 'The' is not used in 'What ...!' exclamations.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
During the festival season, the rural branch is always short ______ staff.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: 'short of' = not having enough of something
solution.explanation: A branch that does not have enough staff is 'short of staff'. The adjective 'short' in this sense takes 'of'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Short in', 'short with' and 'short from' are not used for lacking something. ('Short with someone' means rude or impatient to them, which does not fit staff.)

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
The education loan is repayable ______ sixty equal monthly instalments after the course ends.

solution.concept: Fixed preposition: repay or pay 'in' instalments
solution.explanation: A sum paid in parts is paid 'in instalments': 'repayable in sixty equal monthly instalments'.
steps: Noun: instalments (the parts of the payment)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'On', 'by' and 'with' are not used with 'instalments' in this sense.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the option that correctly fills the blank.
When the highway project ended, the contractor had to ______ fifty temporary workers.

solution.concept: Phrasal verb: lay off = dismiss workers because there is no more work for them
solution.explanation: When a project ends, workers hired for it lose their jobs. An employer who dismisses workers for lack of work 'lays them off'.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Lay down' means put down or establish (rules). 'Lay out' means arrange or spend. 'Lay by' means save for later. None means dismiss workers.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ most of its borrowers are farmers, the cooperative bank's fortunes depend heavily on the monsoon.

solution.concept: 'Given that' = considering the fact that (introduces a reason)
solution.explanation: The bank depends on the monsoon because its borrowers are farmers. 'Given that' introduces this known fact as the reason.
steps: Clause 1: most borrowers are farmers (a fact)
Clause 2: the bank depends on the monsoon (a result)
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Even though' signals a contrast that is not there. 'Unless' makes the fact a condition. 'So that' gives a purpose.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
You may keep the locker ______ you pay the annual rent on time.

solution.concept: 'As long as' = on condition that
solution.explanation: Keeping the locker depends on paying the rent on time. 'As long as' introduces this condition.
steps: Condition: pay the rent on time
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Even though' signals contrast. 'So that' gives a purpose. 'Unless' would mean you may keep the locker only if you do not pay on time.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the connector that best fills the blank.
______ carefully the bank checks its documents, a few clever forgeries will always slip through.

solution.concept: 'However + adjective/adverb' = no matter how
solution.explanation: 'However carefully the bank checks' means 'no matter how carefully it checks'. The result (forgeries slip through) happens whatever the degree of care.
steps: Blank is followed by an adverb: 'carefully'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Moreover' adds a point and cannot be followed by an adverb this way. 'Whatever' goes with a noun ('whatever checks'). 'Although carefully the bank checks' is ungrammatical.

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Combine the two sentences into one without changing the meaning, and choose the option that correctly begins the combined sentence.
The officer checked all the documents. Then she approved the loan.

options.text: Having been checked all the documents,

solution.concept: Perfect participle ('Having + past participle') for the earlier of two actions by the same subject
solution.explanation: The officer did both actions, one after the other. 'Having checked all the documents, she approved the loan' shows that the checking was completed first.
steps: Same subject for both actions: the officer
'Having checked all the documents, she approved the loan.'
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Checked all the documents' and 'After checked' are not complete participle forms. 'Having been checked' is passive and would describe the officer as the one checked.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Having checked all the documents,

questions.subject: English Language
questions.question_text:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
______ than cut jobs during the slowdown, the company reduced the salaries of its top managers.

solution.concept: 'Rather than' = instead of; it can begin a sentence and be followed by a base verb
solution.explanation: The company chose one action in place of another. 'Rather than cut jobs, the company reduced ...' expresses this preference.
steps: Two alternatives: cutting jobs or cutting top salaries
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Instead' takes 'of', not 'than' ('Instead of cutting jobs'). 'Better than' and 'Other than' change the meaning and do not express a choice of one action over another.
